s01: These two leftovers can remember a number.
Group these counters in threes, and two remain.
Regroup the same counters in fives, and three remain.
Suppose you forget the count but keep those two remainders.
Which counts could they describe?
Among zero through fourteen, leaving two after division by three allows two, five, eight, eleven, and fourteen.
Only eight also leaves three after division by five.
This table gives every count a pair of remainders.
The row tells what remains after division by three; the column, after division by five.
Follow eight into row two, column three.
Every cell has exactly one count from zero through fourteen.
Why does the pattern repeat after fifteen?
Adding fifteen adds five complete groups of three, or three complete groups of five.
Neither remainder changes.
So eight, twenty three, and thirty eight all fit the same clues.
Conversely, two counts with the same remainders must differ by a multiple of three and a multiple of five.
Because three and five share no factor larger than one, their difference must be a multiple of fifteen.
The clues identify exactly one count in each block of fifteen consecutive integers.
This is a small case of the Chinese remainder theorem.
Coprime divisors let separate remainders work together.
Without a known range, they remember a repeating family, not one unique integer.

scenes.narration:
These two leftovers can remember a number. Group these counters in threes, and two remain. Regroup the same counters in fives, and three remain.

Suppose you forget the count but keep those two remainders. Which counts could they describe? Among zero through fourteen, leaving two after division by three allows two, five, eight, eleven, and fourteen. Only eight also leaves three after division by five.

This table gives every count a pair of remainders. The row tells what remains after division by three; the column, after division by five. Follow eight into row two, column three. Every cell has exactly one count from zero through fourteen.

Why does the pattern repeat after fifteen? Adding fifteen adds five complete groups of three, or three complete groups of five. Neither remainder changes. So eight, twenty three, and thirty eight all fit the same clues.

Conversely, two counts with the same remainders must differ by a multiple of three and a multiple of five. Because three and five share no factor larger than one, their difference must be a multiple of fifteen. The clues identify exactly one count in each block of fifteen consecutive integers.

This is a small case of the Chinese remainder theorem. Coprime divisors let separate remainders work together. Without a known range, they remember a repeating family, not one unique integer.
